title: The gutka and the steek
hookLine: the small book wrapped in cloth on a high shelf: a gutka, and its bigger sibling, the steek
tomorrow: what are the tiny marks hanging off every letter?
last: PEN AND SWORD · THE WAY · MANY STREAMS.

lines: WRAPPED IN CLOTH, KEPT UP HIGH.
cards: Every family has one object nobody is allowed to throw out: a recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting, a watch that stopped long ago.
In a Sikh home it might be a small book, wrapped in a cloth, kept up high where nothing gets stacked on top of it. Yesterday's question: what is it? It's a gutka.
Small enough for a pocket or a purse, it holds the daily prayers in Gurmukhi: the Japji in the morning, the Rehras in the evening, the Sohila at night.

teach.b: A gutka is small, but nothing in it is small talk. Guru Ram Das says it, in paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word, and inside the Word is all the nectar.

teach.h: THE SAME CARE, SMALL BOOK OR BIG.
teach.b: So yesterday's care doesn't shrink with the book. Clean hands, a covered head, a cloth around it, a place up high. Now its bigger sibling: the steek.

A steek sets the Gurbani on the page and adds commentary beside it, line by line: what the old words mean, how one line leads to the next. The Gurbani stays exactly as it is. The commentary is a helper, not a replacement.
That's worth knowing about every explanation, including the paraphrases on this path: they walk you toward the words; they aren't the words.

teach.h: ONE TO RETURN, ONE TO LEARN.
teach.b: On a phone, a Gurbani app does something like both at once: the Gurmukhi above, a meaning underneath. And here's why the two books belong together.
The gutka is for saying the same prayers every day, until they live in your mouth.
The steek is for understanding, slowly, one line opened up. One keeps you returning. The other keeps you learning.

how: Sikhs read the daily prayers (Nitnem) from a gutka, kept wrapped in cloth and stored respectfully, and study the Granth's meaning from steeks, printed or online, which set commentary beside the Gurbani.

o: a small book of the daily prayers from the Gurbani
a cloth used to wrap the Granth for the night
a commentary explaining each line of the Granth

games.q: small book, big word — tap the pairs.
p: a small book of the daily prayers
the Gurbani with commentary beside it

s: a gutka is an informal copy, so it can be handled casually
small book, big word: it's wrapped and kept up high, with the same care as the Granth.
a steek replaces the Gurbani with an explanation
the Gurbani stays exactly as it is; the commentary sits beside it as a helper.
Guru Ram Das says the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word
so the care doesn't shrink with the size of the book.

games.q: your friend Maya heard a line of the Japji at the gurdwara and wants to know what it means. you have a gutka and a steek. which do you open with her?
o: the steek: the line stays as it is, with commentary beside it to open it up.
the gutka: the smaller book is the more correct one for a question like this.
neither: Gurbani is only for reciting, so its meaning can't be explained.
games.why: the gutka is for saying the prayers every day; the steek is for understanding, one line opened up. one keeps you returning, the other keeps you learning.

practice: If you can, open a gutka, a steek online or a Gurbani app, and rest your eyes on a single line without trying to read it fast: the Gurmukhi letters, the meaning beneath, the space between them.
If you can't, hold or look at one small thing you keep for what it means, the way that book is kept. Breathe slowly, and let that one line, or that one thing, be all there is to see.

wordCard.voice: Gutka. A small book of the daily prayers from the Gurbani, kept with the same care as the Granth's words. The second word of the year.
